chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
title: Decca's poor sound versus RCA's Erskine Hawkins records
summary: McRae fought with Decca over a bad-sounding Ella date after hearing Erskine Hawkins's "Tuxedo Junction" on RCA.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: See now, he probably got two or three other people on his job that's working with him. He probably don't want them on this particular -- He probably want -- this is a date that's set up. This is an all star date that he want to do for this thing (inaudible). He want to sell the records, because -- Now -- and another thing, this is what the sound that he wants. He don't want the sound that he's got -- the music that he's using. And then -- and back in those days, you have to -- See, recording wasn't the best -- See, the studio -- I remember when I recorded with Decca. I used to get so mad with Decca, because I used to fight it every time I go in the studio, because what I was getting out at Decca -- you know, when I want to hear my records back, I

The last date I did with Ella Fitzgerald when I had the band -- I get in from the coast -- I had this beautiful date to do with Ella Fitzgerald. And the band was (inaudible) playing (inaudible). And when I heard the playback, I said, "Man, what are you doing to me? You're killing me!" Something was (Inaudible) happening, you know, they were still learning. All these companies were just learning.
Learning the technique.
Yeah, learning the technique like Decca. They wasn't up. You know, they --
Sound reproduction --
Because they had a studio and one of them would put the drums over here at the door -- they'd put the drums here at certain place or

Did they use the partitions and that sort of thing?
Partitions and all kind of junk like that, you know. And then recording on the wax -- the big wax tape, you know. We recorded on that.
Put them in a great big box. A great big wax tape (Inaudible). And the sound wasn't good.
Now the same time we worked the Savoy with Coleman Hawkins -- Erskine Hawkins Band -- it was a band out of Alabama, you know.
Erskine Hawkins.
Erskine Hawkins came up here and they give him a date -- he got a date on RCA Victor! RCA, you know.

I remember when they made 'Tuxedo Junction' and we just had got a record come out -- well out record come out the same time from Decca -- And when I heard Erskine Hawkins and 'Tuxedo Junction' on RCA, I flipped, because it was a

much better recording than I had, you know. I say, "Man, listen to this. Listen to Erskine. Look how that record sound!" You know what I mean?
So when I went to Decca (inaudible), I said, "Man, yall got to get a better" -- They got one of the best sounding bands in the country and the record don't sound like nothing, you know.

They thought I was crazy. So Moe Gale came over, "Oh, it's all right, don't argue, we'll go through the thing." I was giving them a fit over there. So Moe Gale come over, say, "Teddy's mad about something." I say, "No." I say, "You know that last date we did here, man? How bad it sound? Have you heard Erskine Hawkins record on Tuxedo Junction on RCA Victor, how good that record sound?"
